title: The Twelve, the Strong Man, and Jesus' True Family
summary: Jesus heals a man's withered hand on the Sabbath, and the Pharisees begin plotting with the Herodians to kill him. Crowds pour in from every region, and Jesus appoints twelve apostles to be with him and to be sent out. His family thinks he is out of his mind, scribes from Jerusalem accuse him of driving out demons by Beelzebul, and Jesus answers with the parable of the strong man, a warning about blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and a declaration that whoever does God's will is his brother, sister, and mother.
story: The chapter opens with the last of the five controversy stories that began at 2:1, and it ends that series with a plot to kill Jesus (verse 6). From here the lines are drawn. On one side, huge crowds come from Galilee, Judea, and the surrounding lands, and Jesus forms a new community around himself, the Twelve. On the other, the opposition hardens: religious leaders from Jerusalem accuse him of working with Satan, and even his own family misunderstands. The chapter asks the reader to decide what Jesus' power means, and it redefines who belongs to him. Chapter 4 will explain, through parables, why the same word produces such different responses.
historical:
The setting is still Galilee in the late 20s AD. The Herodians of verse 6 were supporters of Herod Antipas and the Herodian family's rule; that they joined with the Pharisees, whose concerns were religious, shows how widely Jesus was seen as a threat, since Antipas had already arrested John the Baptist. The list of regions in verses 7 and 8 covers nearly the whole of the old land of Israel and beyond: Idumea in the south, the ancestral homeland of Herod's family (the Edom of the Old Testament), the region east of the Jordan, and the Phoenician coastal cities of Tyre and Sidon in the north, which were Gentile territory. Word of Jesus had spread far beyond Galilee's villages.

That scribes came from Jerusalem signals that the religious authorities in the capital were now investigating Jesus. The names of the Twelve are also known from the lists in Matthew 10, Luke 6, and Acts 1, which differ slightly (Thaddaeus here appears as Judas son of James in Luke). Simon is called the Zealot; the Greek form Mark uses comes from an Aramaic word for zealous. It may mean he was zealous for the law, or that he had been associated with those who resisted Roman rule, though the organized party called the Zealots is attested mainly in the war of AD 66 to 70.
cultural:
Choosing twelve was a deliberate sign. Israel was made up of twelve tribes descended from the sons of Jacob, and many Jews hoped that God would one day restore the scattered tribes. By appointing twelve, Jesus acted out that restoration, forming the nucleus of a renewed people of God around himself. Renaming Simon as Peter (meaning rock) and James and John as Boanerges (Sons of Thunder) followed a biblical pattern in which a new name marks a new role or identity.

Family was the center of honor, identity, and economic life in the ancient Mediterranean world, and a son who left his trade to become a wandering preacher, drawing crowds and conflict, brought shame on his relatives. That is the background to their attempt to take custody of him. Jesus' saying that those who do God's will are his family would have sounded radical. Christians have understood the brothers of Jesus in different ways: many Protestants take them as sons of Mary and Joseph born after Jesus; Eastern Orthodox tradition as Joseph's sons from an earlier marriage; and Roman Catholic tradition, following Jerome, as cousins or close relatives. Beelzebul was a name for the prince of demons, probably derived from Baal-zebub, the god of the Philistine city of Ekron (2 Kings 1:2).
literary: The chapter contains one of Mark's characteristic sandwiches. The story of Jesus' family setting out to seize him (verses 20 and 21) is interrupted by the scribes' accusation and Jesus' reply (22 to 30), and then resumed when his mother and brothers arrive (31 to 35). The two stories interpret each other: both family and scribes misjudge Jesus, one saying he is out of his mind, the other that he is possessed, and both are contrasted with those sitting around him doing God's will. Jesus answers the scribes in parables, the first time Mark uses the word, preparing for chapter 4. The strong man image is the key: Jesus' exorcisms are not Satan's work but proof that someone stronger has come to bind him and plunder his house.

outline.t: A withered hand healed on the Sabbath; the plot begins
Crowds from every region and spirits silenced
Jesus' family thinks he is out of his mind
The Beelzebul accusation and the strong man

doctrines.note: Jesus appoints the Twelve to be with him and to be sent out, the two movements of the church's life. He redefines his family as all who do God's will, forming a community bound not by blood but by obedience to God.
The parable of the strong man interprets Jesus' exorcisms as the invasion of Satan's house by one stronger. God's kingdom arrives as a liberation of those held captive by evil.

Jesus promises forgiveness for every sin and blasphemy, with one warning: those who call the Spirit's work in him evil put themselves beyond forgiveness. The warning is aimed at hardened opponents, not at the anxious or doubting.

words.note: Apostolos, apostle, one who is sent, a messenger with authority to represent the sender. Jesus designates the Twelve apostles because they will be sent out to preach and drive out demons. The word later extends to others, such as Paul, commissioned by the risen Christ.

Porosis, hardening or hardness, used of a heart that has become insensitive. Jesus is angry and grieved at the hardness of heart that would rather see a man stay crippled than see a rule bent. Mark later uses related language even of the disciples (6:52, 8:17).

Ischyros, strong or mighty. John the Baptist announced one more powerful than himself (1:7), using the same word. In the parable Satan is the strong man, and the implication is that Jesus is the stronger one who binds him, an image with roots in Isaiah 49:24-25.

Blasphemia, blasphemy, speech that slanders or insults, especially God. The scribes accused Jesus of blasphemy for forgiving sins (2:7); now Jesus warns them that attributing the Spirit's work to Satan is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit.

christ: The chapter shows Jesus as the stronger one who has come to bind the strong man and free his captives, fulfilling Isaiah's promise that the Lord would take captives from the mighty (Isaiah 49:24-25). The unclean spirits recognize him as the Son of God. He acts like Israel's God in choosing and naming twelve, as God chose the twelve tribes. He grieves over hard hearts and looks with love on those who do God's will. And the plot to kill him in verse 6 shows that his path to the cross is already set. The one who binds Satan will do it finally not by exorcism alone but by his death and resurrection.

hard.q: What is the unforgivable sin, and could someone commit it without knowing?
hard.a: Jesus says that all sins and blasphemies will be forgiven except blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, and Mark explains the context: the scribes were saying Jesus had an unclean spirit (verse 30). In other words, they looked at the Spirit's plain work of liberation and called it Satan's. Most interpreters understand the sin not as a single careless word but as a settled, willful rejection of God's work in Jesus, a refusal of the only source of forgiveness. It is unforgivable not because God's mercy runs out, but because the person has shut the door through which forgiveness comes. Pastors have long noted that people who fear they have committed this sin show, by their very fear and desire for God, that they have not. The warning is addressed to hardened opponents, and the chapter's main note is the breadth of forgiveness: all sins and blasphemies will be forgiven to the sons of men.

questions: Jesus called the Twelve first to be with him, then to be sent out. How do those two callings relate in your own life?
Jesus' family and the religious experts both misjudged him. What wrong conclusions about Jesus do people draw today, and what drives them?
Jesus says whoever does God's will is his brother, sister, and mother. How should that shape the way Christians treat one another, especially those without family?
